parole.testo: Literally, “an apple and an egg”. From Low German and/or Central German; see Appel (“apple”). On farms, apples and eggs were often the most numerous produce, so they were very cheap. Cognate with Dutch een appel en een ei.

parole.significato: to obtain through slyness or quickness; to wangle
parole.testo: From ab- + luchsen. The latter from Low German lucksen, intensive form of luken, from Middle Low German lūken (“to pull, to pluck”), from Proto-Germanic *leukaną, which is related to Locke (“curl”, originally “tuft of hair”). In Standard German it was associated with an originally unrelated verb luc

parole.significato: to fob off, to get rid of a request, a caller, visitor etc., often by means of pretext
parole.testo: 19th century. Ostensibly from ab- (“off”) + wimmeln (“to teem, to move in a confused crowd”). The meaning could perhaps be understood as “to keep such a crowd away, move out of it”. However, a more satisfying interpretation as “to wave aside” can be based on cognate Low German wiëmeln, wemeln, which
Partial calque of Low German Achterdeel. By surface analysis, achter- (“hind-”) + Teil (“part”).
From acht (“eight”) + Kante (“edge”) + -ig. The adverbial use is probably a pun on Low German Achterkant (“backside”, hence “buttocks”).
Via Low German Appelsina, from Dutch appelsina (cp. appelsien, for which now usually sinaasappel). So named because of their introduction to Europe from China (Latin Sīna).

parole.significato: to run off, to abscond (especially of pets and livestock escaping their encosure or home)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German utbücksen. Possibly through Bangebüx (“scaredy pants”). By surface analysis, aus- + Buxe

parole.significato: to sheer, sheer out (move away from a course, leave a formation)
parole.testo: 19th century, from nautical parlance, from Low German utscheren. By surface analysis, aus- (“out”) + scheren (“to escape”).

From Low German Bangbüx(e); analysable as bang (“afraid”) + Büxe, the latter being a rarer variant of Buxe (“trousers, pants”). Compare Angsthase (thought to be an alteration of *Angsthose), Dutch bangebroek, English shit one's pants.
Borrowed from Low German bannig.
Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German barsch (“sharp, pointed, strict (in taste)”), from Old Saxon *barsk, from Proto-Germanic *barskaz, from *barsaz (“bass, perch”).

parole.significato: need (that which is desired or required)
parole.testo: From Low German and Middle Low German bedarf, the present stem of bedörven (“to need”), from Old Saxon bi- + tharvōn (“to need, lack, want”). Morphologically identical to the present singular of Middle High German and German bedürfen.
From bei + gehen, chiefly a calque of Low German bigahn.

The contemporary form since the 19th century from Low German bibbern, probably already Middle Low German *bibberen, a frequentative of bēven (from Old Saxon bibōn, bivon), from Proto-West Germanic *bibēn, cognate of modern German beben. Compare Dutch bibberen (1700), English biver. In spite of the l
From Low German and Middle Low German blinken, ultimately from the root of blecken (“to bare”). Cognate with Dutch blinken.

parole.significato: to bleat, to baa (make the sound of sheep and some other animals)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German bleken, ultimately imitative.
Via Low German and Middle Low German bodden (alongside bodem and other variants), from Old Saxon bodom. Doublet of Boden.
Borrowed from Low German Bolltje, diminutive of Boll (“roundish object”), from Proto-Germanic *bullǭ. Equivalent to Bolle (“bulb, tuber”) + -chen. Cognate with Dutch bolletje, Danish bolsje.
Low German [Term?]

parole.significato: small meadow or plot of grass, often slightly hilly or elevated; village green
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German Brink, from Middle Low German brink, from Proto-Germanic *brinkaz. Cognate with Dutch brink, English brink.
17th century, from Low German, from Middle Low German bucht, from Old Saxon buht, from Proto-West Germanic *buhti, from Proto-Germanic *buhtiz. Cognate with Dutch bocht, English bight.

parole.significato: to dig, especially with one’s hands or paws
parole.testo: 18th century. Variant of a Low German and Central German verb (pudeln, puddeln); see pudeln (“to splash, dabble”). The contemporary form seems to have spread from Berlin.

parole.significato: to play (a slot machine or video game)
parole.testo: 20th century, from Low German daddeln, also dadeln, tateln (“to stutter, gabble, cackle”), of onomatopoeic origin. Compare archaic German dadern, Dutch tateren, tatelen, English tattle. Originally said of the choppy sounds of slot machines.
Probably from Low German dase (“stinging fly”).
From Deich (“dyke”) + Low German Schart (“notch, cleft”), a partial calque of Low German Diekscha(a)rt n, from Middle Low German dîk + schārt.
Borrowed from Low German. Further origin unknown. Speculations include a relation with French tête(s).

parole.significato: nomen vicis of drehen: a turn, spin, twist, a single rotation
parole.testo: Deverbal from drehen, after Low German Dreih m (compare Dutch draai). Chiefly since the 19th century, earlier attestations are isolated. Widely displaced older Drehe f. The sense “trick” is from Rotwelsch (thieves’ cant).

parole.significato: violent stream or swell (of the sea)
parole.testo: Low German doublet of Trift (“path on which livestock is driven”). From Middle Low German drift, from Proto-West Germanic *drifti, from the verb *drīban, whence German treiben (“to drive”). Compare English drift.
Low German drömen (literally “to dream”).
Borrowed from Low German duun.

parole.significato: athwart, abreast (to the side of a ship)
parole.testo: 19th century, borrowed from Low German dwars, from Middle Low German dwers. Doublet of quer, the main form (from Central German), and obsolete zwerch (from Upper German), still in Zwerchfell.

Formally from Low German Düker, from Middle Low German düker (“diver”, also “culvert”?). Doublet of Taucher ("diver"). The sense “culvert” may be a loan translation of Dutch duiker. At least its adoption into standard German was probably reinforced by Dutch.

parole.significato: swell (series of waves, especially after a storm)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German Dünung, from dunen (“to expand”), probably related to Dumen (“thumb”), for which see Old Saxon thūmo.
Borrowed from Low German edderdune, from Icelandic æðardúnn. By surface analysis, Eider + Daune.
19th century, from Low German. Analysable as ein- + Bucht + -en. In Low German, Bucht also means a “pen for livestock”.

From Low German and Middle Low German erpel, which is borrowed from Middle Dutch erpel (introduced by Flemish settlers in the East), probably a pet form of the Old Saxon personal name Erpo or Old High German Erpho (literally “the brown one”), from Proto-Germanic *erpaz (“brown”). The word is not par
Borrowed from Low German [Term?].

Spread during the 20th century from Low German, Low Franconian, and Central Franconian dialects, from Middle Low German vīs and early modern Dutch vijs, respectively. Compare contemporary Dutch vies (from a dialectal form), West Frisian fiis. Per Pfeifer a connection with Latin spīrō (“to breathe, b

From Low Franconian and Low German dialects along the Dutch border, which it entered (before 1930) from Dutch fiets, perhaps partly through Dutch Low Saxon fietse. Further origin uncertain. In an alternative theory, the direction of derivation went the other way. See the Dutch etymology.

parole.significato: a large room containing the hearth, located between the barn or threshing floor (Tenne, Diele) and the living room or p…
parole.testo: From Low German Flett, from Middle Low German vlet (“ground, flat surface”), from Proto-Germanic *flatją. Cognate with English flet, related with the adjective flat.

parole.significato: fluff, lint of fabric, wool, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German Fluse, from Middle Low German vlūs (“sheepskin”) or a derivative thereof, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *fleus (“fleece”). The same word from an earlier borrowing is Flause (“illusion”), making these doublets along with Flausch.

parole.significato: to sprawl, to lounge (to situate or have situated oneself in a relaxed, careless, non-upright manner)
parole.testo: From Fläz (“lazybones”) + -en in the 2nd half of the 19th century, from Low German Fläz of unknown origin. Perhaps through Münster region vläts (“a loathsome person”) from Proto-West Germanic *wlātiþō or derived from the name of the theologian Matthias Flacius. Küpper instead connects the verb to Mi

parole.significato: to fiddle; to move something in one's hands, especially by rubbing it between thumb and forefinger
parole.testo: 20th century, from Low German and Central Franconian dialects. Cognate to Dutch friemelen (“to fiddle, fidget”). Probably the same as Dutch and Middle Dutch wriemelen (“to move back and forth”, intransitive and transitive), Low German wrimen (“to rub”), with a development from wr- to fr-, which is w

parole.significato: to cheat, usually at a game
parole.testo: From Low German fuddeln (“to work negligently”) and Central Franconian fuddele (“to work negligently; to cheat; to use contraception”). The verb may be derived from Low German Fudde, Central Franconian Fudd, Fuddel, all “rag, old cloth” (compare Dutch vod); plausibly through a sense “to brush superf

parole.significato: hooch, booze, swill (liquor of low quality)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German Fusel, perhaps originally from Rotwelsch. Cognate with English fuzzle (“to make drunk, intoxicate”).

parole.significato: firth, fjord, a long, narrow bay of the sea
parole.testo: From Low German Föörd(e) (“ford, shallow water, firth”), from Middle Low German vȫrde, byform (perhaps originally plural) of vōrt, from Proto-Germanic *furduz. Doublet of inherited Furt (“ford, river passage”) and of Fjord (“fjord”), from Old Norse fjǫrðr. This latter may also have influenced the se

parole.significato: a kind of pastry comparable to poffertjes and Berliner
parole.testo: From Low German Futtje. Possibly from futt (“at once, directly”), cognate of High German fort (cf. sofort). The form Förtchen is probably based on this interpretation, but it is also plausible because the pastries are baked in batches and then directly eaten. Alternatively it could be related with D
18th century, from Low German Gaffel, from Middle Low German gaffele, from Proto-West Germanic *gabulu (“fork”). Doublet of Gabel.

From Low German Ganter, from a merger of Middle Low German gante and ganre, respectively from Proto-Germanic *ganutô and *ganzô. The former is cognate with Middle High German ganze (whence the southern Ganser), Dutch gent, English gannet. The latter is cognate with English gander.
Low German, from Middle Low German gest, from Old Saxon *gest, from, from Proto-West Germanic *jestu. Compare Dutch gist, English yeast, Swedish jäst, Icelandic jöstur.

From Low German Gössel n or f (18th c.), from Middle Low German *gösel (unattested, but certain, because diminutive -el is not productive in the modern dialects). Analysable as German Low German Goos (“goose”) + -el.

parole.significato: a lagoon behind a spit or narrow island, especially in the Baltic Sea
parole.testo: Ca. 1800, from Low German Haff, from Middle Low German haf, from Proto-Germanic *habą (“heaving sea”). Cognate with Old English hæf and Danish hav.

parole.significato: dumbbell, barbell (weight with two disks attached to a bar)
parole.testo: 19th century, from an infrequent Low German dialect word, which was spread (like several others) by Jahn. Pertaining to Hand (“hand”).

From Low German and Middle Low German harsch, from Proto-Germanic *harskaz; see also Russian короста (korosta, “to itch”), Old Church Slavonic краста (krasta), Lithuanian karsiu (“to comb”). Compare English harsh, which is also borrowed from Middle Low German.
Borrowed from Low German Heister, from Middle Low German hēgester, from Old Saxon agastria, from Proto-West Germanic *agastrijā. Doublet of Elster.
Borrowed from Low German Hellinge, from Middle Low German hellinge, heldinge, from the verb helden (“to tilt, to hield”), Proto-Germanic *halþijaną.

parole.significato: to heave (lift and move something with great difficulty)
parole.testo: Ca. 1800, in nautical parlance, thus perhaps through Low German, eventually from English heave, from Middle English heven, from Old English hebban, from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan. Doublet of heben and kapieren.

parole.significato: to squat; to crouch; to sit in a huddled position
parole.testo: From Low German and Middle Low German hucken, from Proto-Germanic *hukkōną (“to squat”).

From Low German Holster, from Middle Low German holster, from Old Saxon *holster, from Proto-Germanic *hulistrą. The word was borrowed directly from Low German (early 19th c. or earlier), but remained rare until the later 20th c., when it was reinforced by English holster, itself of Low German origi

parole.significato: to hop (especially referring to a hare)
parole.testo: From Middle High German hoppeln, iterative form of hoppen. The latter is formally a Low German and Central German variant of hüpfen (“to hop”) (from Middle High German hüpfen or hupfen; it is also present, however, in Alemannic dialects (where it may be borrowed from the North or formed independentl

parole.significato: carried on someone’s back (particularly another person); piggyback
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German Huckeback, as in enen up’n Huckeback nömen (literally “to take someone on one’s piggyback”). The first component is cognate with German Hucke (“load, burden”) or a related verb hucken (“to carry a load”). The second component is from Middle Low German bak (“back”) by the con
Borrowed from Low German ick, ik. Doublet of ich.
Borrowed from Low German ick, from Proto-Germanic *ek, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm.

From Low German jolle, from Middle Low German jolle, possibly ultimately from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewlos (“tube”), see also Lithuanian aulas, Norwegian aul, Hittite [script needed] (auli-, “tube-shaped organ in the neck”), Albanian hollë, Latin alvus.

Derived from Low German, from Middle Low German Jurian (compare Dutch Jurriaan, Swedish Örjan), from Latin Geōrgius (which see for cognates), from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (Geṓrgios), whence also Georg, Jörg.

19th century, from Low German Kaat, Kate, from Middle Low German kāte, a late spelling of kōte, from Old Saxon *kota, from Proto-West Germanic *kotā, from Proto-Germanic *kutǭ ~ *kutą (“stall, tent”), whence also Dutch kot, English cot, cottage. The a-spelling reflects the merger of â, ā, ō into /ɔː
Borrowed from Low German, from Dutch kous (“stocking”). Cognate with Danish kovs.

Borrowed from Low German Kerbe, from Middle Low German kerf, kerve, probably related to Old Saxon kervan (“to cut”). Synonymous with Kerbtier (1815 by Lorenz Oken); cf. German Low German half (“half”) and Dutch half (“half”) with High German halb (“half”).
Borrowed from Low German kilhalen, adapted to German holen. Compare Dutch kielhalen.

From Low German kilswīn, borrowed from Swedish kölsvin, from older Swedish kölsvill (“keel tie”), of which the first element is from Old Norse kjǫlr and the second element from syll. Compare Dutch kolzwijn, Danish kjølsvin, Norwegian kjølsvin, Norwegian Nynorsk kjølsvill.

Probably from Low German killern, apparently iterative of *killen, kiddeln, from Middle Low German kittelen, kētelen, from Old Saxon kitilōn, from Proto-Germanic *kitilōną. For the phonetic development compare especially Danish kilde, kildre, Norwegian kile. Also cognate with German kitzeln, Dutch k

parole.parola: Kinder, die was wollen, kriegen was auf die Bollen
parole.significato: a phrase used to teach children that they should say ich möchte or ich hätte gern (“I’d like”) instead of ich will (“I…
parole.testo: Literally, “children who want something get something on their thighs / buttocks”. Probably a calque from Low German. The anatomical use of Bollen is especially Westphalian, where the phrase is attested in 1912 as Kinner, die wat wollen, kriegt wat op den Bollen (note that wollen is preterite in thi
An originally Low German and Central German word of uncertain origin. Possibly derived from Kippe (etymology 1).

Borrowed from Low German, probably kleppen (“to strike rapidly, ring with a sharp sound”) (referring to bells on the harness), probably ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *klappōn (“to strike, clap”).

parole.significato: to fight, to engage in a fistfight
parole.testo: Central and Low German form (and doublet) of klopfen (“to knock”). The verb was adopted into standard German, in its rougher sense, via the modern vernaculars. An older standard word is the derivative Klöppel (“clapper”). Cognate with Dutch kloppen.

parole.significato: synonym of Kandiszucker (“rock sugar”), especially to sweeten tea
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German Kluntje, diminutive of Klunte.
18th century, from the verb kneifen, after Low German Kneep, from Middle Low German knēp (“trick”). Compare Dutch kneep.

Borrowed from Low German Knuust, from Middle Low German knūst. Compare Dutch knoest and knuist. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénus (“cheek, jaw, chin”) and its synonymous derivative *ǵn̥h₂dʰ(h₁)-. Then cognate with Latvian zods (“chin, sharp edge”), Lithuanian žándas (“cheek”) and Ancient Gree
Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German kogge. Ultimately from the root of Kugel (“ball, orb, globe”). Compare Kocke; also Middle Dutch kogge, French cogue.

Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German krabbe. Cognate with Dutch krab, English crab, Old Norse krabbi (Norwegian krabbe, Swedish krabba). Ultimately from the same root as krabbeln. See crab for more.

Borrowed from Low German Kribbe, from Middle Low German kribbe, from Old Saxon kribbia, from Proto-West Germanic *kribbjā, from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ. Doublet of Krippe (“crib”). For the sense compare Dutch kribbe, which also has it; perhaps originally referring to the crib- or trough-shaped spaces

parole.significato: to list (to lean towards the sides or rotate around the long axis, of ships or similar vessels)
parole.testo: According to Duden, borrowed from Low German krengen, in turn from Dutch krengen. Whether borrowed or inherited, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *krangijaną.
Krug (“pub; bar”) + -er (“-er”) or Low German Kröger (“innkeeper”)

From Low German Köm (“caraway”), contracted (as [køːm] < [køːmm̩] < [køːmn̩]) from older Kömen, from Middle Low German kȫmen, from Proto-West Germanic *kumīn, from Latin cuminum, from Ancient Greek κύμινον (kúminon). Doublet of Kümmel.
Borrowed from Low German Köter, from Middle Low German kȫter. Standard use since the 18th century. Further origin uncertain. Perhaps imitative of panting.

parole.significato: groyne, breakwater (structure built perpendicular to the shore to prevent erosion)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German, from Middle Low German lāne (“alley”). Cognates include English lane.

18th century, from Low German lasch, from Middle Low German lasch, las, from Old Saxon *lask, from Proto-West Germanic *laskw, from Proto-Germanic *laskwaz (“dull, lax, sluggish, lazy”). Likely influenced by French lâche, from Latin laxus.

parole.significato: appetent, or fond of sweets right now or as a habit
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German leckerfritzig.

parole.significato: hatch (opening in the ceiling/floor of a room, in the deck of a ship, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German, from Middle Low German lûke, from Old Saxon *lūka, from Proto-West Germanic *lūkā. Cognate with Dutch luik (“hatch”) and, more distantly, doublet of Loch (“hole”) and Lücke (“gap”); see the former for more.

parole.significato: to look, glance; (especially) to peek, spy
parole.testo: From Low German luuschern, iterative of Middle Low German lûschen (“to lie in ambush”). Probably cognate with High German lauschen (“to eavesdrop, listen closely”).

parole.significato: synonym of Herrengedeck (“a glass of beer served with a glass of Korn”)
parole.testo: From Low German. The first element is a variant form of lütt (“little”).

parole.significato: mad, crazy, not quite right, whimsical
parole.testo: From Low German mall, from Middle Low German mal, of uncertain origin. Cognate with Dutch mal.

parole.significato: stone dead, dead as a dodo, dead as a doornail
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German mursdōd, interpreting mu(r)s (“suddenly, entirely”) as Mūs (“mouse”) (New High German Maus) through folk etymology. Compare Dutch morsdood.

parole.significato: a turbid refuse of liquid, swill
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German Miege (“piss”), deverbal from miegen (“to piss”), from Proto-West Germanic *mīgan (“to piss”).

parole.significato: clamp (heap of potatoes or other root vegetables stored under straw or earth)
parole.testo: Low German [Term?], Latin mēta (“cone”).
A Low German variant of Muff.
From Low German Mull, from Middle Low German mul, mol. Cognate with Dutch mol, English mole. Related with German Molch (“salamander”).
Borrowed from Low German molm, compare Dutch molm.

parole.significato: to sip; to take a nip
parole.testo: In the standard language since the 17th century. From Central and Low German dialects, respectively from northern Middle High German *nippen and Middle Low German nippen, from a Proto-West Germanic *hnipp-Vn, expressive variant of *hnīpan (“to pinch”). Cognate with older Upper German nipfen, Dutch n

parole.significato: to gripe, whinge (complain in a whining tone)
parole.testo: From Low German nölen, whence also Dutch neulen, Danish nøle. The sense "gripe" is derived from "speak slowly or lengthily", itself perhaps from "dawdle" (though it might be the other way round). Further origin uncertain, but usually considered onomatopoeic.
18th century, from Low German Nüster, from Middle Low German nüster, noster. Related to Nase (“nose”).
From Low German pack, from Middle Low German pak, from Old Saxon *pakko, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô. Akin to, and possibly borrowed from, Dutch pak.

Occasionally since circa 1800 from Low German paddeln (“to scurry, tottle, dabble, splash, twitch”), frequentative of padden, padjen (“to step, scurry, walk in shallow water”). Probably from a variant of Middle Low German pedden (“to tread, tramp”), cognate with Dutch pedden, Old English pæþþan, whi
From Low German, from Middle Low German pâl (“stake, post”) + stēke (“stitch, knot”), equivalent to standard German Pfahl + Stich. Compare Dutch paalsteek.

From Low German pardu(t)z, from Middle Low German pardûs, ultimately onomatopoeic. The form with -au- occurs first in Campe’s writings and might be a mechanical adaptation to the Standard German vocalism. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål bardus, Dutch pardoes, perdoes, Swedish burdus, and Danish bardus

parole.significato: level (measurement of how high something is filled)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German Pegel, from Middle Low German pēgel, from Proto-West Germanic *pagil. Cognate with English pail.

parole.significato: smudgy, mucky (covered with sticky dirt or fat residue)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German pekig, derived from Middle Low German pek (“pitch”), which is cognate with German Pech.
Possibly a variant of pimpern, from Low German pümpern (“to crush in a mortar”), from Middle Low German pumpen (“to beat, thump”).

From Low German püükfien, tautological compound of püük + fien, both roughly “excellent, fine, clean, honest”. The former is a borrowing from Dutch puik, from Middle Dutch puuc, from Old Dutch *puiken, from Proto-West Germanic *pūka, *pūga, from Pre-Germanic *pūkk, of uncertain origin, possibly Prot

parole.significato: to torment, to bully with small but repeated acts
parole.testo: From a Low German dialectalism Ossenpesek (literally “ox pizzle”) from Pese (“tendon”), Peserik (“rod”), as a pizzle was used in the 18th century to beat man and animal.
Probably borrowed from Low German pümpern (“to crush in a mortar”), from Middle Low German pumpen (“to beat, thump”). Compare Pimmel.
Borrowed from Low German Pinkel, perhaps from Pink (“pinkie, penis”); compare Dutch pink.

parole.significato: to pour down heavily and loudly
parole.testo: From Low German pladdern, with shortening before -er- (as e.g. in verheddern) from Middle Low German plāderen. Cognate with Middle Dutch pladeren (dialectal Dutch plaaieren, plaren). Ultimately of onomatopoeic origin; compare plätschern, prasseln.

parole.significato: a kind of seasoned and smoked sausage made from pork and beef, similar to cervelat or salami
parole.testo: From Low German Plockwost. For the first element there are three explanations: (1) from Middle Low German plock, pluck (“post, stake”), cognate of German Pflock, due to its shape, which is reminiscent of a fence post; (2) from a variant of Block (“block”); (3) from a Low German word for “lump of fat
From Low German pral, from Middle Low German pral (literally “to bounce, spring back”), ultimately related to prallen (“to collide”).

Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German brassen, probably related to the root of Swedish brasa (“small fire”), French braise (“live coals”), comparing boastful behavior to the sound of roasting food.
18th century, borrowed from Low German Priel, whence also Dutch priel. Further origin unknown.
From Low German and Middle Low German prunk, probably related to the root of prangen (“to show off”).

parole.significato: grounds, sediment (residue in or from a liquid, especially coffee)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German and Low Franconian dialects, ultimately of imitative origin. Compare Dutch prut.
From Low German, probably onomatopoeic.
Borrowed from Low German Pull(e), from Middle Low German appulle, from Latin ampulla. Doublet of Ampel and Ampulle. Compare Dutch pul (“tankard”).

parole.significato: a type of sourdough rye bread with a strong, sweetish flavor; coarse, brittle, and dark in color; native to north-weste…
parole.testo: 17th century, from Westphalian Low German Pumpernickel (literally “farting Nicholas”), originally attested in the sense “coarse, clumsy bloke”. From pumpern (“to fart”) + Nickel (diminutive of Nikolaus). The use for the bread alludes to its being coarse-ground and particularly its flatulent effect.
From pusseln, pöseln (“to do petty work”) + -ig, variants of bosseln borrowed from Low German.

parole.significato: a blowball, dandelion clock (seedhead of dandelion)
parole.testo: Attested 19th century, chiefly from Low German dialects. Analysable as pusten (“to blow”) + Blume (“flower”), from the children’s habit of blowing off the seeds. However, this may be only a remotivation of an underlying dialectal Pissblume, from the dandelion's diuretic effect; compare Dutch pisbloe
Borrowed from Low German or Dutch potsig (“funny, cute”), which belongs to Old French bocer.; related to Butz (“goblin”).
Borrowed from Low German Pütt, from Middle Low German pütte, from Old Saxon putti, from Proto-West Germanic *puti (“a well”). Doublet of Pfütze (“puddle”) and Pütz (“well; bucket”).

parole.significato: to eat or drink casually instead of by reason of nutritional need
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German püttkern (“to handle liquids, to draw or scoop them up (schöpfen) or to drink”), also pöttkern, from Pott (“pot”) and + -kern (“denoting a repeated activity, often of lesser intensity”).

parole.significato: jabber, natter, palaver, yap, gab, jaw, twaddle, rattle on, rabbit on (to talk a lot or talk nonsense)
parole.testo: Late 19th c., from Low German quasseln, variant of dwasseln, iterative of Middle Low German dwāsen (“to talk nonsense”), from dwās (“dim-witted, daft”), from Old Saxon *dwās, from Proto-West Germanic *dwās. This adjective is cognate with Middle High German twās, Dutch dwaas, Old English dwǣs.

parole.significato: heifer (young cow that has not calved)
parole.testo: From Low German Quene, from Middle Low German quēne (“old woman, hag”), from Old Saxon quena, from Proto-West Germanic *kwenā (“woman”). The sense probably developed from “barren cow” (cf. Dutch kween, also attested in Low German dialects) via “calfless cow” to “young cow”. Doublet of Kone, which wa

parole.significato: glasswort, pickleweed (Salicornia, kind of edible plant growing in salt marsh)
parole.testo: From Low German Queller, from Middle Low German queller, quelder. Cognate with Dutch kwelder (“salt marsh”). Probably from quellen (“to soak, swell with water”) + -er.
19th century, from Low German. Analysable as quick (“lively”) + Born (“well”).
Borrowed from Low German Rabauke, diminutive of Rabau (“rogue, scoundrel”), from Dutch rabauw, from Middle Dutch rabaut, from Old French ribaut. See ribald
From Low German Racker (“privy cleaner”, also “scoundrel”), from racken (“to scrape, sweep”).

parole.significato: to make dull and/or guttural sounds
parole.testo: From Low German rallen (“to talk, chatter”), from Middle Low German rallen, likely of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Danish ralle, which has the same sense as the Modern German.

18th c., from Low German, from Middle Low German ramponēren, from Middle Dutch ramponeren (whence Dutch rampeneren), from Old French ramposner (“to taunt”), of uncertain derivation. The semantic development under influence of Middle Dutch ramp (“harm, calamity, catastrophe”).

parole.significato: to jostle, scrap, wrestle (fight physically without dealing serious blows)
parole.testo: 18th century, from Low German, from Middle Low German rangelen (“to wrestle”), iterative of rangen, byform of wrangen (“to struggle”). Cognate with English wrangle. Related with German ringen (“to wring one's hands”), auswringen (“wring out”), from Proto-Germanic *wringaną. The irregular loss of ini
From Low German and Middle Low German recke (“crossbar”), ultimately from the root of Rah (“yard”). Cognate with Dutch rek (“pole, clothes-horse”).
Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German rēde, akin to Plautdietsch reed (“ready”), from Old Saxon *girēdi, from Proto-West Germanic *(ga)raidī, from Proto-Germanic *raidaz.
Borrowed from Low German Reet, from Middle Low German rêt, from Old Saxon hriod, from Proto-West Germanic *hreud.

parole.significato: reef (part of a sail that can be rolled in during high wind)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German Reff, from Middle Low German ref. Cognate with Dutch reef, English reef, Danish rev. Further origin uncertain. The West Germanic forms are possibly borrowed from Old Norse rif. If so, the word may identical to that for “rib” (Proto-Germanic *ribją), from which is also German

parole.significato: to reef (shorten a sail in high wind)
parole.testo: Circa 1700, from Low German reffen, derived from Middle Low German ref. See Reff for more.

parole.significato: railing or balustrade on a ship
parole.testo: From Low German Reling, Regeling, derived from Middle Low German rēgel, from Old Saxon *rigil, probably from Latin regula, though this sometimes doubted. Cognate with German Riegel, Dutch richel, and possibly English rail. The form Reling was reinforced and standardised under the influence of Englis

parole.significato: groove (narrow channel; often one of several parallel ones)
parole.testo: Via Low German/German Low German from Middle Low German rīve (“rake”), ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *hrīban (“to rake, scratch”). Cognate with Dutch rijf (“rake”), Old Norse hrīfa (“rake”), Old English hrīfnian.

Borrowed from Low German robbe, rubbe, in Middle Low German meaning “rabbit." Of uncertain ultimate origin; compare English rabbit, French rabot (“plane”). Or, possibly related to Latvian rups (“coarse, rough”), referring to the whiskers. Also compared is the personal name Robbe. Has also been compa
From Low German Rüümte, from Middle Low German rūmte; perhaps also influenced by cognate Dutch ruimte. Analysable as raum (“wide”) + -te; compare geräumig. Also cognate with English roomth.

parole.significato: jabber, gab, rattle on, rabbit on (to talk a lot and quickly, or to talk nonsense)
parole.testo: Related to sabbern (“to drivel, drool”). This word entered standard German alongside sabbern from Low German [Term?]. Subsequently, the meaning of this term shifted; sabbern retains the original meaning, "drool". Compare southern Dutch zabberen, standard Dutch sabbelen. The nouns Sabber and Sabbel a

Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German sabben, ultimately from the source of Saft (“juice, sap”). Closely related to sabbeln (“to babble”). Compare southern Dutch zabberen and standard Dutch sabbelen.

16th c., borrowed from Low German sacht, sachte (“soft”), from Middle Low German sachte, from Old Saxon *sāfti, from Proto-West Germanic *samft(ī) (compare Proto-Germanic *sōmiz (“agreeable, fitting”)), from Proto-Indo-European *sóm-tu-, possibly from *sem- (“one, whole”). Doublet of sanft. Cognate
Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German sacken, from or related to Old Saxon sinkan (“to sink”). Compare Dutch zakken.

parole.significato: a low burrow in which hares rest and hide themselves
parole.testo: From East Low German sassen (“to sit, settle”), for which see sitzen.

parole.significato: template, stencil (physical object used for replicating outlines)
parole.testo: 18th century, from Low German Schablun, Schabbelun, from Middle Low German schaplūn, earlier schampeliōn (“pattern, shape, model”), from Middle Dutch schampelioen, from Middle French eschantillon, from Old French eschandillon (“standard”), from Vulgar Latin *scandiculum, derived from Latin scandula

parole.significato: cupboard, cabinet, especially a simple one, e.g. a locker
parole.testo: From Low German Schapp, from Middle Low German schap, from Proto-Germanic *skapą. Doublet of Schaff.

parole.significato: dock worker who loads and unloads ships, lumper
parole.testo: 19th century, from Low German Schauer, from Dutch sjouwer, derived from sjouwen, from West Frisian sjouwe.

With -au- by artificial adaptation to standard German from Low German Schukel, a lengthened variant of Low German Schuckel (also early modern German Schuckel), deverbal from schuckeln, schockeln, iterative of Middle Low German and Middle High German schocken, from Proto-West Germanic *skokkōn. Relat
Borrowed from Low German, from Middle Low German schēmeren or Middle Dutch schemmern, intensive form of schemen (“to flash, blink”), ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *skīnan (“to shine”).
Low German, schinden (“to skin”) + Luder (“carrion; bait”)

parole.significato: to go by ship, to sail (usually slowly)
parole.testo: From Low German, from Schipper (“captain, one in charge of a boat”), from Middle Low German schipper, alteration of schēper, from Proto-Germanic *skipārijaz, whence also German Schiffer. Compare Dutch schipperen (“to manoeuvre, sort out, cope”).
From Low German Schitt(e), Schiet(e) (“shit”), from Middle Low German schīte, from Old Saxon *skiti, from Proto-West Germanic *skiti. Cognate with German Scheiße. See shit.
Borrowed from Low German slackern.

parole.significato: something on someone’s back by which they are grabbed in order to push or pull them: the collar, the hem of the jacket,…
parole.testo: 18th century, but probably older. Generally explained as a reinterpretation (as a diminutive) of Schlafittichen, dative plural of obsolete Schlafittich, itself from an underlying *Schlagfittich, from schlagen (“to strike, thrash”) + Fittich (“wing of a bird”), from the way a bird is grabbed by its t
Borrowed from Low German slidderen. Doublet of schlittern.

parole.significato: to braise, to stew (cook in a covered pot in a small amount of liquid)
parole.testo: From Low German and Middle Low German smôren, from Proto-Germanic *smurōną (“to suffocate, strangle”), probably related to *smallijan (“to burn”) or Old English smoca (“smoke”). Cognate with Dutch smoren, English smother.
Either a deverbal from schmuggeln or directly borrowed from Low German smuggeln.
Borrowed from Low German smuggeln, from Middle Low German smugen, from Proto-West Germanic *smeugan (“to slip through, creep”). Compare Swedish smyga. Cognate with English smuggle, also a borrowing.

parole.significato: to be fried or baked slowly, making a sizzling sound
parole.testo: From Low German smorkeln, smurkeln (“to seethe, sizzle, smoulder”), iterative of smorken (“to smoulder”), derived from smoren (“to burn slowly, to braise”), whence German schmoren, probably through a blend with smoken (“to smoke”) (see Schmauch). Possibly introduced into literary German, and at leas

parole.significato: book, tome (typically big or old and not particularly gripping, but suited for casual, cozy reading)
parole.testo: From Low German Smöker, from the verb smöken (“to smoke”), from Middle Low German smöken, from Proto-West Germanic *smaukijan. The semantic motivation is unclear. Some compare Schinken (literally “ham”) and thus interpret Schmöker as “smoked ham”. Others compare Swedish lunta (literally “fuse”) and

parole.significato: bric-a-brac, knick-knack (miscellaneous items of little import)
parole.testo: Reduplication; from schnacken or Low German schnacken (snacken) (“chatter”) (compare Plautdietsch schnaken (“chatter”)).
From Low German snikke (“pretty”), influenced by schniegeln (“to spruce up”).

parole.significato: to chop; to cut into small pieces (e.g. vegetables)
parole.testo: Frequentative of schnippen + -eln, from Central and Low German dialects (18th century). Compare Dutch snippen (“to chop”).
Northerly Central German or Low German consonantism from Proto-Germanic *snuttuz.

Early 20th century, deverbal from Low German schnorgeln, snörgeln (“to snore, snuffle”, attested 19th century). So called because of the stertorous sound. Related to schnarchen (“to snore”). Doublet of obsolete Schnörchel (“a certain disease of pigeons”).

parole.significato: a wry or contorted mouth, especially a pout, moue (way of pushing out one’s lips)
parole.testo: 18th century, from Low German Snute, from Middle Low German snûte, from Old Saxon *snūt, from Proto-West Germanic *snūt. Doublet of Schnauze (“snout, muzzle”), which is an earlier (adapted) borrowing from the Low German.

parole.significato: a young man who is brash and presumptuous
parole.testo: 19th century, from Low German Snösel, Snäsel (18th c.). The sense “snotnose”, which Pfeifer considers original, is of very limited attestation and not mentioned at all by early sources such as the Low German dictionaries of Dähnert (1780) and Schütze (1806). Nevertheless it is plausible to associate
From Low German Schot, from Middle Low German schot, ultimately from the root of schießen (“to shoot”). Cognate with Dutch schot.
Borrowed from Low German.

18th century, from Low German swelen, from Middle Low German swēlen, from Old Saxon *swelan, from Proto-West Germanic *swelan, from Proto-Germanic *swelaną (“to smoulder, burn slowly”), from Proto-Indo-European *swel- (“to shine, warm, burn”). Cognate with Dutch zwelen, Old English swelan. Also rela

Borrowed from Low German, from Middle Low German swōl, swūl, in Standard German since the 18th century, ultimately from the root of schwelen (“to smoulder”). The umlaut is possibly due to analogy with kühl (“cool”). The unumlauted form schwul is limited to the sense “gay, homosexual”. Cognate with D

Ca. 1700, from Low German Segge, from Middle Low German segge, from Old Saxon *seggi, from Proto-West Germanic *sagi, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaz. Cognate with Dutch zegge, West Frisian sigge, English sedge, Scots seg.
18th century, from Low German Siel, from Middle Low German and Old Saxon sīl. Cognate with Dutch zijl, West Frisian syl.
Borrowed from Low German.

18th century, borrowed from Low German Spant, extended form of Middle Low German span, deverbal from spannen. Comparable with High German Gespann (“that which is clamped, fastened; hence, team of horses, oxen”). Compare Dutch spant.
Low German form of Spinnwebe (“cobweb”).

20th century, from Low German Spliss, Spließ, from the nautical verb splissen (“to splice; to fray the ends of ropes and tie them together”). The latter is cognate with Dutch splitsen (“to split”, older also splissen) and related with Proto-Germanic *splītaną, whence regional German spleißen (also u
Borrowed from Low German sprott.
From Low German and Middle Low German spōken; equivalent to Spuk + -en. Cognate with English spook and Dutch spoken.

Borrowed from Low German Stack, from Middle Low German stak. Probably related with stāke (“stake”). Possibly influenced by stacket (“stockade, picket fence”), itself from also related Old French estakete.
Of native dialectal origin (common especially in Low German), from Medieval Latin stante pede, whence also the literary loan translation stehenden Fußes, which see for more.
Low German and Central German in form (Middle Low German stempel). This northern form replaces Middle High German stempfel from Old High German stemphal. Pertaining to stampfen (“to stamp”).

From rare Middle High German stiur, reinforced by Low German Stüür, both from Middle Low German stǖr, from Proto-Germanic *stiuriją, from the verb *stiurijaną. In general use since the 18th century. Cognate with Dutch stuur, English steer.
From Low German and Middle Low German stotteren, iterative of the verb stōten (“to bump, nudge (the tongue when speaking)”), from Old Saxon stotan.

parole.significato: a northwestern German, especially Westphalian, kind of yeast-based pancake, comparable to a crumpet, traditionally eate…
parole.testo: From Low German Struwe, from Middle Low German strûve (“flat pastry”), from the adjective Proto-Germanic *strūbaz (“stiff, shaggy”). Doublet of southern Straube (“kind of fritter, doughnut”). Further cognate with Dutch struif (“pancake, omelette”).
19th century, from Low German, from Middle Low German stubbe m, from Proto-Germanic *stubbô.

parole.significato: viscous as a result of long cooking or the addition of a thickening agent
parole.testo: Central and Low German form which (since the 19th c.) has displaced the slightly earlier seimig (18th c.). Equivalent to archaic Seim (“viscous liquid”, especially “syrup, honey”) + -ig. The spelling with -ä- (instead of -e-) could represent West Central German dialects, but is more probably analogo

18th c., from Low German Teckel, a variant of German Dackel, also Dächsel and perhaps *Däckel, from Dachshund. Most readily explained as a borrowing from Upper German or East Central German dialects, which use the diminutive ending -el and in which word-initial ‹d› tends to be voiceless. Note, howev
Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German ter, from Old Saxon *tero, from Proto-West Germanic *teru, from Proto-Germanic *terwą.

From Low German Titte (“nipple; breast”), from Middle Low German, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *titt- (“teat; nipple; breast”); according to Pokorny, this is ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tata- (“father; parent; nipple”), though this is uncertain. In any case, all are of expressive origin.

parole.significato: Indicates agreement, especially of an arrangement or a wager.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German topp, perhaps related to Middle Low German toppen (“to beat”).
From Low German, compare Dutch trappen.

From Low German treck, from Middle Low German trek, from Old Saxon *trekan, from Proto-Germanic *trekaną, *trakjaną (“to drag, haul, scrape, pull”), from Proto-Indo-European *dreg- (“to drag, scrape”). Cognate with English trek.

parole.significato: to tow a ship or boat along a river or canal (usually by means of horses)
parole.testo: 18th century, from Low German treideln, alteration of Middle Low German treilen, from Middle Dutch treilen, from Old French trailler, derived from the noun traille, from Latin tragula.

Late 18th century, from Low German Trieze (also Tritze, Trisse, Trietsche), from Middle Low German tritze, trisse (vowel short and long). Cognate with Dutch trijs, English trice. Further origin unknown.

parole.significato: to disturb or annoy someone, especially in order to provoke a reaction; to goad
parole.testo: From Low German tritzen (and variants). Equivalent to Trieze (“winch”) + -en. The modern sense is figurative from the nautical punishment.

20th century, from Low German tuckern (“to throb, pulsate”, 19th c.), iterative of tucken (“to jerk, twitch, beat, hit”), which is cognate with Dutch tokken, tukken, German zucken, zücken, and thus ultimately related to ziehen (“to pull”). The semantic development within Low German as well as the ad
From Low German and Middle Low German tūten, of imitative origin (lautmalend).

17th century, from Low German Töle. Further origin uncertain. Plausibly from an old, though unattested, diminutive of Middle Low German tō (“bitch, female dog”), in the form of an Old Saxon *tōhila. The Middle Low German is cognate with archaic German Zohe (“bitch”), perhaps related with ziehen (“to
Literally, “around that turn”. Dreh is here probably used in the regional (East Central and Low German) sense “turn of a road, bend in a path”. Compare synonymous die Ecke (literally “that corner”).
From um + zu, after Low German ümto.

First attested around 1900, borrowed from Low German unbedarvd (“clumsy”), from Middle Low German unbederve, unbedarve (“weak, clumsy”), ultimately from Middle Low German bederven, bedarven (“to need, to require”).

parole.significato: cultivable, arable, prepared for agricultural (or rarely silvicultural) use
parole.testo: In the modern sense (18th century) via Low German from Middle Low German *ōrbār (in ōrbārheit), Middle Dutch ōrbare (“fruitful”), derived from the noun ōrbār, from Old Saxon ur- + beran (“to bear”), cognate of modern German Urbar (“urbarium”, originally “yield, benefit, fee”), which see for more. An

parole.significato: to lose or forget something out of carelessness or forgetfulness
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German verbaseln (chiefly reflexively “to lose one’s way”, but also as in Standard German), an iterative-diminutive of verbasen (“to baffle, confound”), from Middle Low German vorbāsen. Cognate with Dutch verbazen, Norwegian forbause, etc.

From Low German, from underlying God verdor(r)e di/ju, which means “may God make you lose your mind”, related with Tor (“fool”), or alternatively “may God make you wither, shrivel”, related with verdorren (“to wither”). Compare Dutch verdorie.

18th century, borrowed from Low German verheddern, derived from Middle Low German hêde (“tow, hards”), from Proto-West Germanic *heʀdā. By surface analysis, ver- + Hede + -ern. The shortened vowel is due to the influence of -er- (as in Mutter and various other words).
Verklicker (“fly on the top of a ship showing wind direction”) + -n, from Low German. A similar notion is found in zeigen / wissen woher der Wind weht.

Borrowed from Low German verquars, variant of verdwars, derived from ver- + dwars (“cross, diagonal, aslant”), from Middle Low German dwers, dwer, from Old Saxon thwerh, from Proto-Germanic *þwerhaz. Doublet of synonymous verquer. The final -t in German (or perhaps already Low German) by association

From vorschlagen (“to strike first”) + Hammer (“hammer”). It seems originally to have meant a smaller hammer used by the foreman to indicate the places where the other men must hit. The modern sense may be from confusion with (1.) Low German Vörhamer (Middle Low German vȫrehāmer, cf. English foreham
Borrowed from Low German [Term?], from Middle Low German warschuwinge (“warning”); altered by folk etymology to a compound of wahr (“true”) + Schau (“look”).

17th century, from Low German, from Middle Low German walnut, from Proto-West Germanic *walhahnut, from Proto-Germanic *walhaz (“foreign”) + *hnuts (“nut”). Cognate with Dutch walnoot, English walnut, and (from Middle Low German) Danish valnød etc. Equivalent to wal- (related with welsch) + Nuss; co
Borrowed from Low German [Term?].

Borrowed from Low German Warf, from Middle Low German warf, werf, from Old Saxon hwerf, probably from hwervan (“to turn around”). The word was first adopted as Werft (17th c.), which became specialized to the sense “shipyard” in High German. Since the 19th century, newer Low German Warf was introduc

parole.significato: a water-filled depression, especially at the back of a dyke
parole.testo: From Low German Wehl, Weel, from Middle Low German wêl. Cognate with Dutch wiel.
Borrowed from Low German Wippe. Compare Dutch wip.
From Low German and Middle Low German wippen, ultimately from or related to Proto-West Germanic *waibijan (“to move back and forth”).

parole.significato: to whisper; to make a whispering sound (most often in a mysterious or eerie way)
parole.testo: 17th century, from Low German wispern, chiefly displacing the above variant, from Middle High German and Middle Low German wispelen, ultimately of imitative origin (lautmalend). The r-form could be a late alteration, but could also be old in view of Old English hwisprian, whence English whisper.

parole.significato: swede, neep, rutabaga (Brassica napus subsp. rapifera)
parole.testo: From eastern Low German (Mecklenburg, Pomerania, West Prussia), perhaps originally meaning “knobby tree trunk”. Further origin uncertain. Occasionally used in standard German since the 18th century. Cognate with synonymous Czech brukev, Polish brukiew, Kashubian wrëk, Ukrainian бру́ква (brúkva), Rus

17th century (standard since ca. 1800), from Low German Wucht (“weight”), byform of Wicht with assimilation of the vowel to the adjacent consonants. Further from Middle Low German wicht(e), from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz. Cognate with English weight.

parole.significato: to lift or turn (something) with a quick, jerking movement
parole.testo: Variant of wippen, and like this a Central and Low German word. In some Low German dialects, wuppen is the regular outcome of Middle Low German wippen (cf. the development in Wucht). In other dialects, the same form was probably derived by playful neo-ablaut.

parole.significato: a dish made of ground, boiled meat cuts (as used in sausage making) and groats
parole.testo: From wursten (“to make sausage”) + Brei (“pap”), a calque of Westphalian Low German Woastebräi.

parole.significato: a kind of sausage or dumpling made from coarse rye meal and blood
parole.testo: From wursten (“to make sausage”) + Brot (“bread”), a calque of Westphalian Low German Wuostebraut. So called because it is a sort of dough (“bread”) that is traditionally prepared after slaughtering.

parole.significato: man-made hill or elevation (as used in low areas to protect farmhouses against flooding)
parole.testo: From Low German Wurt, Wort, from Middle Low German wurt, from Old Saxon wurth, from Proto-Germanic *wurþiz. Cognate with Dutch woerd (“man-made hill”), Icelandic urð (“area covered by fallen rocks”).
Low German seisen (verb)
From Low German sorren, *zorren, perhaps from Dutch tsorren, older variant of sjorren. Further origin uncertain.
Borrowed from Low German.

parole.significato: flamboyant, eccentric; excessively outgoing, bubbly, cheerful, possibly to the point of being shrill, silly, over the t…
parole.testo: Partial calque of Low German överkandidelt (19th c.), from kandidel (“cheerful”), itself plausibly from Latin candidus (“clear, bright”, hence “untarnished, untroubled”).
